scenario:
You have volunteered for a research study about learning and study habits.
You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.question: Thank you for your participation. Today, I'd like to ask you some questions about learning and study habits. First, in your opinion, how do people your age prefer to study—alone, in groups, or with a mix of both?
questions.modelAnswer: I think people my age often prefer a mix, but many start alone. Solo study helps them focus on reading and problem sets without distraction. Group study is popular before exams when friends want to compare notes. Overall, I would say most students combine both depending on the subject and the deadline.
evaluationPoints: Addresses study preferences of people a similar age
Chooses alone, groups, or a mix
Gives at least one reason or example
Stays on topic within the time limit

questions.question: I see. And when you have an important exam coming up, do you usually make a detailed plan, study a little each day, or focus intensively at the last minute?
questions.modelAnswer: When I have an important exam, I try to study a little each day. A detailed long plan can feel overwhelming, but daily review helps me remember better. I start with lecture notes, then practice questions closer to the exam. I avoid pure last-minute cramming because I get too stressed and forget details.
evaluationPoints: States a clear personal exam-prep habit
Chooses planning, daily study, cramming, or a mix
Explains why that approach works for the speaker

questions.question: Interesting. Many people say that digital tools have changed how students learn. Do you think online resources make learning more effective than in the past? Why or why not?
questions.modelAnswer: Yes, I think online resources can make learning more effective than in the past, if students use them carefully. Videos, practice apps, and discussion forums explain difficult ideas in many ways. Students can review anytime. The risk is distraction and shallow skimming. Still, compared with limited textbooks alone, good digital tools give more chances to understand and practice.
evaluationPoints: Takes a clear yes/no or nuanced position

questions.question: Good points. I just have one more question. Some people believe that learning from teachers in person is the most important part of education. Do you agree, or do you think students can learn equally well in other ways? Why?
questions.modelAnswer: I partly agree that in-person teachers are very important, but students can also learn well in other ways. A good teacher can answer questions immediately and motivate a class. However, well-designed online courses, books, and peer study groups can be highly effective too. The best education often combines teacher guidance with independent learning.
evaluationPoints: Responds clearly to the agree/or-other-ways frame
Gives a reason for the chosen position
May mention teachers and alternative learning paths
